query: For Q235 steel in its pre-exposure state, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain the onset or suppression of corrosion-related degradation in harsh environments at room and elevated temperatures? Specify a controlled study that would isolate the governing cause, predicted observations relative to the untreated reference, applicable boundary conditions, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification result.

generation.hypothesis: The native, self-forming iron oxide film on Q235 steel governs the onset or suppression of corrosion in harsh, chloride-containing environments. A robust, chemically stable oxide layer suppresses further corrosion, whereas a mechanically or thermally compromised oxide film promotes localized corrosion by exposing active metal sites.
generation.material_initial_state: Q235 steel in its as-received (pre-exposure) state with its naturally formed thin native oxide film and inherent microstructural heterogeneities (e.g., grain boundaries and inclusions)
generation.intervention: Apply a pre-treatment that modifies the native oxide layer—either by mild oxidizing annealing to reinforce the oxide or by mechanical cleaning to partially remove it—followed by controlled exposure to a 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution at room temperature and at an elevated temperature (e.g., ~100°C).
generation.conditions: Samples will be exposed under identical chloride-rich conditions with controlled temperature (room temperature and ~100°C), humidity, and exposure time. The only difference between samples will be the pre-treatment to alter the oxide film’s integrity.
generation.structural_mediator: The chemical composition, thickness, and continuity of the native iron oxide film that forms on Q235 steel surfaces.
generation.mechanism: Under benign conditions, the intact native oxide acts as a passivating barrier, reducing metal dissolution. However, in aggressive environments or when the oxide film is compromised (either by mechanical removal or thermal stress), the protective barrier is disrupted, leading to accelerated corrosion via enhanced anodic dissolution at exposed sites. Conversely, an intentionally reinforced oxide film (via mild oxidizing anneal) is expected to provide better protection, slowing the degradation process.
generation.predicted_outcome: Samples with a reinforced (thicker, more uniform) oxide layer will exhibit lower weight loss, reduced pitting density, and higher electrochemical impedance compared to untreated Q235 steel. Conversely, samples where the oxide film is partially removed or disrupted will show accelerated corrosion relative to the untreated baseline.
generation.baseline: Untreated Q235 steel exposed under the same chloride-rich and temperature-controlled conditions, representing the natural behavior of the native oxide film.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies only to low alloy carbon steels like Q235 in which the native oxide film is the primary corrosion-influencing interface. Effects may not translate to highly alloyed steels or those with deliberately engineered surface coatings.
generation.uncertainty: The exact thickness, composition, and microstructural attributes of the protective oxide layer that optimally suppress corrosion are not fully quantified. The magnitudes of the corrosion rate differences under varied oxide conditions are also currently uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare three sets of Q235 steel samples: (1) untreated (baseline with native oxide), (2) samples pre-treated with a mild oxidizing anneal to reinforce the oxide layer, and (3) samples mechanically cleaned to remove the oxide film. Expose all samples to a 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution under two temperature regimes (room temperature and ~100°C) for a fixed time period. Measure corrosion rates by weight loss, electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS), and analyze surface morphology (via SEM) and oxide composition (via XPS).
measurements: Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy to assess barrier properties
SEM imaging to quantify pitting density
XPS analysis to characterize oxide composition and thickness
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If there is no statistically significant difference in the corrosion metrics (weight loss, pitting density, EIS response) among the three sets, or if the reinforced oxide samples do not demonstrate improved corrosion resistance relative to the untreated samples, the hypothesis that the integrity of the native oxide film governs the corrosion behavior is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: In this paper, CrMnFeCoNi HEA coatings with different ZrC contents were prepared on Q235 steel by a PTA process, and the effects of ZrC on the morphology, composition, hardness, friction, and corrosion properties of the coatings were investigated.
